lead: On the day the Panchangam remembers Most Rev. Isaac Mar Yoohanon, the Epistle begins, “Remember your leaders”, and the Gospel speaks of the servant whom the master puts in charge of his household. Both readings are about faithful service while the Lord seems to delay. Between them stands the sentence that holds every generation together: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” The key words are remember and faithful.

r.h: Remember your leaders; we have an altar
set: Chapter 13 is the practical close of Hebrews: love of the brethren, hospitality, care for prisoners, faithfulness in marriage (13:1–6). Today's verses turn to the community's leaders, past and present, and then to worship. The readers seem to have been tempted by teachings about special foods, perhaps linked to the meals and rules of the old temple worship. Hebrews answers by pointing to Christ's sacrifice, offered outside the city.
str: vv. 7–8: remember your leaders; Christ is always the same.
vv. 9–10: not strange teachings about food: we have an altar.
vv. 11–14: the sin offering burned outside the camp; Jesus suffered outside the gate; let us go out to him.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifices of praise and of sharing.
kw: Those who go ahead and guide. The leaders of verse 7 have already finished their course; those of verse 17 are still watching over the readers. Both are to be honoured.
The place of sacrifice. Hebrews says that Christians are not people without an altar. The Fathers and the Church have read this verse of the altar of Christ's sacrifice and of the Eucharist.
A phrase from the Psalms (Psalm 50:14, 23). Praise and good works are called sacrifices because they are offered to God through Christ, the one high priest.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
Remembering is not nostalgia. It means looking at how they lived and ended, and copying their faith.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Leaders pass; the Lord they served does not. This is why the faith they handed on is still true for us.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.
On the Day of Atonement the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). The Gospels agree that Jesus was crucified outside the city (John 19:17, 20).
For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.
The Christian is a pilgrim. This does not make him careless of the world; it leaves him ready to serve it.
ch: The Church has read “we have an altar” of the altar on which the one sacrifice of Christ is made present in the Eucharist (CCC 1365–1367). The sacrifices of praise and of sharing in verses 15–16 flow from that altar into daily life; they do not replace it. The Catechism teaches that the Church prays for the faithful departed, and above all offers the Eucharistic sacrifice for them (CCC 1032). So on this day we remember a shepherd of our Church, thank God for him, and pray for his rest.

set: Chapters 24–25 of Matthew are Jesus' last great discourse, spoken on the Mount of Olives a few days before his death. He speaks of the end of the temple and of his coming at the end of the age. Since no one knows the day or the hour (24:36), the discourse turns to a series of parables about readiness. Today's follows the short saying about the thief in the night (24:43–44); tomorrow's parable of the ten bridesmaids comes next.
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise servant?
vv. 46–47: the blessing of the servant found at work.
vv. 48–51: the wicked servant who says, “My master is delayed”.
kw: Faithful means reliable when no one is watching; wise means seeing what really matters. The same word for “wise” describes the bridesmaids who took oil (25:2).
The servant's excuse. The same verb is used of the bridegroom in the next parable (25:5). The early Church knew the experience of waiting, and Jesus teaches that the delay is a time for faithfulness.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
The servant is a steward over fellow servants. The Fathers often applied the parable to bishops and priests, who are to feed God's household with the word and the sacraments.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
The blessing is not for one who calculates the date, but for one found doing his ordinary task.
and he begins to beat his fellow slaves, and eats and drinks with drunkards,
When the master seems far away, authority turns into abuse. Jesus warns those who serve that their office is a trust, not a possession.
ch: The Church reads the parable first as a word to all who hold office in her. The Second Vatican Council describes the bishop as one sent to serve and to feed the flock, after the example of the Good Shepherd (Lumen Gentium 27). It is also a word to every Christian, for each of us has been put in charge of something: a family, a work, a gift. The strong ending in verse 51 is Matthew's way of saying how serious it is to betray such a trust.

qa: Why do we pray for bishops and priests who have died?

Because the Church prays for all the faithful departed. Even holy shepherds may need purification before they see God, and our prayer, above all the Holy Qurbono, helps them (CCC 1030–1032). To pray for them is also to thank God for what we received through them.
rite: Today the Panchangam keeps the memory of Most Rev. Isaac Mar Yoohanon, a bishop of our Church, who entered his rest in 1987. It also offers John 10:11–18, John 14:1–6 or John 15:9–17 as Gospels that may be read on this memory. In our tradition the names of the departed shepherds are remembered in the Holy Qurbono, and Hebrews 13:7 tells us why: their faith is a lamp for ours.
study: Who first spoke the word of God to me? How can I imitate their faith this week?
What has the Lord put me in charge of? Would he find me at work if he came today?
